## LLM Recipe

### 1.2 Model Architecture &amp; Scaling Laws

#### [Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14423>)

This work fits multimodal pretraining laws that account for directional transfer, competition for model capacity and diminishing returns from repeated vision or audio data. Controlled mixture-of-experts experiments make the framework useful for planning how to divide a training budget among model size, unique data and modality mixtures, while requiring coefficients to be fitted for the intended setup.

**Published:** 2026-10-10 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:36:31.851Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Scaling Laws, Multimodal Pretraining, Data Mixtures

**Public availability:** 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14423>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The October 14 new-submission batch and official schedule imply public availability at October 14 00:00 UTC, despite the October 10 submission date. Sections 2–6 and Appendices G–I cover 268 fitting experiments and three held-out runs; eight of nine held-out modality-loss predictions are within 2.6% of observed values.

**Limitations:** Coefficients depend on tokenizers, discrete next-token objectives, data quality and sparse architecture. The non-text-heavy continuation underpredicts text loss by 6.73%; larger-scale and video validation remain future work. Loss prediction is not a downstream-capability guarantee, and no code release or independent reproduction was verified.

### 1.7 Reinforcement Learning &amp; Reasoning

#### [Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18853>)

Two Clocks separates the samples needed for learning progress from those consumed before training collapse when rollout batches and learning rates are scaled together. Its controlled GRPO experiments motivate starting below a critical batch size and increasing the batch later, helping practitioners evaluate sample efficiency and stability separately from hardware throughput.

**Published:** 2026-10-13 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:36:31.851Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** RLVR, Batch Scaling, Training Stability

**Public availability:** 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18853>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Availability is inferred from the October 14 primary-category new-submission batch and official schedule. Sections 3–6 and Appendices B, F and G test 512–8,192-response batches, clipping and batch ramps on Qwen math models; larger batches lose sample efficiency above a learning-rate-dependent critical scale.

**Limitations:** The local quadratic progress model and drift-threshold failure hypothesis are conditional approximations. Most runs use a modified 1.5B math recipe with KL, entropy bonuses and gradient clipping disabled; robustness settings have limited seeds. The author-linked code repository returned 404, and no end-to-end throughput gain was established.

## AI Agent Dev

### 2.3 Context Engineering &amp; Memory

#### [Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18784>)

CarryOn organizes an agent's context around versioned reusable task objects, explicit unfinished obligations and a recent interaction tail, folding history only after evidence and consistency checks. This lets long-running agents continue from work already present in files or application state; matched Claude Opus 4.7 experiments improve OSWorld 2.0 partial score by 5.8 points while reducing total tokens by 51.9%, including context-management calls.

**Published:** 2026-10-13 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:39:34.000Z · **Novelty:** material-update · **Tags:** Context Engineering, Versioned State, Long-Horizon Agents

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The detailed paper is in the October 14 batch, whose 00:00 UTC availability is inferred from the dated listing and official announcement schedule. October 13 repository preview history contains earlier headline results, although commit times do not prove first public visibility. Sections 3–4 and Appendices A–C add candidate/evidence binding, atomic folds, 40-task ablations and explicit resource accounting. Matched OSWorld 2.0 partial score rises 43.9% to 49.7%, binary success 15.7% to 19.4%; 100 BrowseComp-Plus questions rise 49% to 56%.

**Limitations:** Only one principal host model, one 100-question browsing subset and small 40-task ablations; no independent reproduction. Grounder checks establish scoped consistency and availability, not semantic task correctness. Some comparator scores are previously reported, not matched reruns. ### 2.4 Retrieval &amp; Knowledge Integration

#### [Using specialized data to improve research agent accuracy](<https://parallel.ai/blog/specialized-data-labbench2>)

Parallel compares the same research agent with public-web access alone and with additional PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov connectors on 288 LABBench2 questions. Structured specialist access yields 12 net additional correct answers and illustrates how constrained search, complete records and web-to-database handoffs can improve evidence retrieval even when similar data is publicly indexed.

**Published:** 2026-10-13 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:39:34.000Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Structured Retrieval, Data Connectors, Controlled Evaluation

[Blog](<https://parallel.ai/blog/specialized-data-labbench2>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. The dated October 13 primary report specifies matched agent/model/processor configurations, 168 LitQA3 and 120 TrialQA questions, unchanged benchmark scoring and inspected call traces. Errors change 34 to 22 overall; 15 questions improve and three regress. Connector calls complement web searches for literature questions and often substitute for general lookups on trial records.

**Limitations:** Vendor-authored study with one run per question per condition, no reported confidence interval or repeated-seed analysis, and no isolated attribution across search-space and representation changes. Only two biomedical benchmark subtasks were tested; extrapolation to private legal/financial databases is speculative. Fixed per-question pricing is not a measurement of underlying compute. No paper or released experiment code was verified.

### 2.5 Agent Learning &amp; Skill Acquisition

#### [ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18484>)

ReTerm teaches terminal agents to recover from their own failed environment states, first using teacher-generated repair demonstrations and then mixing ordinary and recovery rollouts during reinforcement learning. Its bounded queue of recent failure states keeps recovery practice aligned with the evolving policy; the authors' matched 9B-model evaluation improves Terminal-Bench 2.0 from 20.2% to 34.8% Pass@1.

**Published:** 2026-10-13 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:39:34.000Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Recovery Training, Agent Reinforcement Learning, Terminal Agents

**Public availability:** 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18484>) · [Code](<https://github.com/twothsnd/ReTerm>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. October 14 batch; arXiv submission October 13 at 14:44:24 UTC. Sections 3–4 describe pre-verifier VM snapshots, teacher-only SFT loss and separate group normalization for original/recovery tasks. Table 4 reports 25.8% for recovery SFT, 28.0% for standard GRPO and 34.8% for ReTerm-GRPO. Three alternative harnesses retain 6.7–12.4-point gains; accessible implementation history begins with October 14 05:52:49 UTC initial release.

**Limitations:** The principal study uses Qwen3.5-9B trained on 16 A100-80GB GPUs, verifier-based synthetic terminal tasks and a fixed evaluation seed. Most other model comparisons come from original papers/releases and are not matched reruns. Recovery analysis uses model judging with manual verification; except tool-use errors, recovery rates remain at or below 32%. No independent experiments were reproduced.

## AI Training &amp; Inference Infra

### 3.2 RL &amp; Rollout Infrastructure

#### [Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16592>)

Prorsa monitors agent trajectories, sandbox startup and tool execution to forecast short-term prefill and decode demand, then switches rollout workers between the two roles. This adapts disaggregated inference to multi-turn reinforcement learning, reducing interference and cache-capacity bottlenecks; the authors report 1.11–4.05x faster agentic rollouts, with slowdowns in most tested single-turn math settings.

**Published:** 2026-10-12 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:36:43.360Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Agentic RL, Prefill Decode Disaggregation, Workload Prediction

**Public availability:** 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16592>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3–5 inspect workload characterization, lifecycle prediction and adaptive allocation atop Verl/SGLang. Experiments use FP8 Qwen3-235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V3.2 and MiMo-V2.5-Pro on a 16-server, 128-GPU cluster with NVLink and 400-Gbps RDMA NICs, comparing rollout time against prefill-decode colocation. Role switching adds 1.0–1.44x over task-tuned static splits in the MiMo ablation. The October 12 v1 submission predates its verified October 14 announcement batch.

**Limitations:** Rollout speedups do not measure full training time or final policy quality. Results depend strongly on attention parallelism and task mix; KV transfer and switching can hurt single-turn workloads. Decode allocation forecasts admission-cache volume without explicitly predicting output lengths or near-term cache reclamation. GPU model and a dedicated code release were not verified.

### 3.3 Inference Engines &amp; Serving

#### [FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18451>)

FastEEP resizes expert-parallel MoE serving instances by reusing worker processes, communication structure and address-stable runtime state while changing which GPUs actively participate. This lets a running service release or reacquire individual GPUs with shorter reconstruction delays; the authors report 4.5–11.7x faster resizing than their vLLM Elastic EP baseline on supported comparisons.

**Published:** 2026-10-13 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:36:43.065Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** MoE Serving, Elastic Expert Parallelism, Runtime State Reuse

**Public availability:** 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18451>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3–6 describe persistent-parent NCCL subgroups, NIXL peer masks, CUDA virtual-memory offload and coordinated worker transitions. Six MoE models are evaluated on two eight-H20-3e nodes with NVLink and 400-Gbps RDMA; resizing takes 4.2–13.4 seconds, while the compared vLLM Elastic EP takes 36.4–92.0 seconds. ShareGPT experiments also measure service interruption, distinct from overall scaling latency.

**Limitations:** This is a 16-GPU evaluation, not demonstrated hundred-rank scaling. Expansion remains bounded by the initialized maximum topology and available memory; dormant state consumes host memory. Resizing still interrupts token output. The Elastic EP baseline cannot run two of the six models, so its speedup range excludes those comparisons. A specific open-source repository or PR was not verified.
